title: Ordered batching
questions: Explain [8,5,3] at capacity 12 and [15,2] at capacity 12. Why does 3 not skip ahead of 5? Why does 15 not block forever?

slide.title: Keep queue order and accept an oversized first item
slide.narrative: The weight limit applies only after the batch has one item. This rule lets an oversized first item leave the queue. Later items cannot pass a front item that would exceed the limit. Thus, a returned batch can exceed capacity, but selection does not skip items to fill unused capacity.

fileSummaries.summary: Batch selection preserves queue order and applies the weight limit only after it accepts the first item.

inlineExplanations.text: The empty batch accepts its first item regardless of weight. After that, `break` stops selection at the first item that would exceed capacity; later items cannot pass it.

svgIllustration.title: The first item moves; the next item controls the stop
svgIllustration.assumptions: Weights are illustrative. Queue position shows order, not weight or time. Each row is a separate call with capacity 12.

plan.question: Why can 3 not pass 5, and why does 15 not block selection?
plan.visualApproach: Show two aligned queues beside their batches. Move each first item into its batch, then show the stop condition at the next item.
plan.whyThisForm: Stable queue positions make the preserved order visible. Separate batch totals show why the same stop rule produces both results.
plan.encodings: Items on the left are pending, with the front item first. The right boundary contains the batch. Numbers are weights; item sizes do not represent weight.
plan.motion: Move 8 and 15 from their queue fronts into their batches. Keep all other items fixed. After arrival, show why selection stops at 5 and 2.
plan.prediction: At capacity 12, [8,4,3] accepts 8 and 4, then stops before 3 because the limit permits equality.
plan.restingState: Both returned batches, their totals, the remaining queues, and the two stop calculations remain visible.

frames.caption: The nonempty condition is false, so neither first item triggers the stop rule.
